en: — *Ṣaḍaṅgasādhana* (The Sadhana of the Six Limbs). Tōh. no. 1239.
Dergé Tanjur, vol. NYA, folios 126v.2–130r.3. Translated by Ratnaśrījñāna and Śākya ye shes.
[206v6] Homage to glorious Hevajra!

To Hevajra— the lord of the eight goddesses who are like the moon reflected in the waters of the illusory mandala— whose faces, feet, and arms are emanations of the suchness that is the reality of liberation;
and to the festival of his activity for the sake of sentient beings, performed upon the delightful stage of the chest of Māra.
Having assumed a grand display, he performed a world-encompassing dance upon the genuine substitute for the sky.
Having bowed with reverence to the Guru, who is like the supreme emanation-body of the Buddha and the sole vehicle for crossing the ocean of saṃsāra, I shall now enter [this work].
The Hevajra Tantra, resembling a vast ocean.
May this practice of the glorious Hevajra, which has come down through the lineage of the feet of Ḍombī, serve as the collyrium that removes the blindness of those blinded by the film of ignorance.
And at night in one's own home,
with the thought "I am accomplished," one should meditate on this without hesitation in a cremation ground or on a riverbank.
One should visualize the syllable HŪṂ upon a solar disc in the lotus of the heart;
one should worship the Gurus and Vajras and perform the seven purifications.
Then, one should emanate the eight goddesses, beginning with Gaurī, for the sake of worship;
thus, one reveals the sin committed and desists from what ought to be done.
One should rejoice in merits, perform their dedication,
go for refuge to the Three Jewels, and cultivate the mind of awakening.
One should rely upon the path and dedicate oneself for the sake of others;
one should seek permission and meditate upon the four divine abodes.
First one should cultivate loving-kindness, and secondly one should develop compassion.
In the third [dhyāna], one should cultivate sympathetic joy; [in the fourth], equanimity in its entirety.
And again, while meditating on the awakening to emptiness, one should utter this:
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness.
In the void, within a lotus and sun disk, he meditates on the universal vajra born from the syllable *hūṃ*,
radiant with the *hūṃ* syllable that quivers as it pierces the hosts of Māras in the world.
Uttering the syllables "Oṃ rakṣa 2 hūṃ 2," one should thereby visualize the vajra-fence, the canopy, and the ground.
In the element-realm, the vajra-ground, one should meditate upon the syllables yaṃ raṃ vaṃ laṃ as the mandala of the elements,
with the syllable bhrūṃ as the vajra above; and within that, one should meditate on oneself as the intermediate state being (antarābhava),
surrounded by these four mandalas with the wheel as the fifth.
Having become blended there, it becomes the Buddha-abode, which is beyond the ordinary range [of perception].
It is square, with four doors, adorned with four archways,
provided with necklaces and half-necklaces, and beautified by eight pillars.
One should draw a single enclosure containing an eight-petaled lotus, where the pedestal for the deities shines with the radiant array of light from the eight goddesses.
Seated within the orb of the sun, he is resplendent with the four Māras.
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra-abode of all Tathāgatas.
The manifestation of the Buddha’s abode consists of the fivefold cultivation of forms;
the moon possesses the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), and the sun possesses the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*).
The inspection of one's own deity by means of the seed-syllables is called the "sign";
the performance of all [these stages] as one is the nature of the manifestation of the image.
One should meditate on the moon with the letter Ā, and on the sun with the letter KĀ.
The interval between these two is HŪṂ; from those two arise the vajra and the razor.
All this has become one— the seed-syllable of the moon and sun, like milk and water inseparable; with that, one meditates upon the Wielder of the Vajra,
who tramples the four Māras and performs the dance in the half-lotus posture.
He is adorned with a necklace of severed heads and has another head topped with a universal vajra.
His principal face is intensely black, the right is like a kunda flower,
the left is red and most terrifying, and the remaining faces are like bumblebees.
He has sixteen arms, eight faces, and four terrifying feet;
the hero wears a garland of skulls, with Nairātmyā embracing his neck.
The deity wears the five mudrās and possesses the luster of a moonstone gem;
his principal face resembles a lotus, the left is red, and the other [right] is white.
Likewise, elephants, horses, donkeys, cows, camels, humans, deer,
and *śarabhas* are to be known as the two-legged and other [animals], positioned in sequence upon the eight southern skull-bowls.
Earth, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Tejas, Candra, Bhāskara,
Antaka, and Dhanada are indeed upon the skull-bowl of Savya’s left hand.
The goddess has two arms and one face; she is dark-complexioned with tawny hair standing erect on her head.
She holds a flaying knife, a skull-cup, and a khaṭvāṅga staff, and is clothed in a tiger skin.
Oṃ! O Lotus, support of bliss, great passion, giver of happiness!
O you who partake in the four joys, O Universal One, perform my task, hūṃ hūṃ!
Oṃ! O Vajra of great hatred, bestower of the four joys, whose singular flavor is the beak of the sky-goer, O Lord, hūṃ hūṃ, accomplish my task!
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra that impassions all Tathāgatas.
Then, having meditated upon the Primordial Being, one should cause the circle of ḍākinīs to radiate forth.
One should perform the passion of the vajra and cause the Victors to hear it swiftly;
those eight seeds became the drops of the Tathāgatas.
One should emanate the goddesses from the seed-syllables Gaṃ, Caṃ, Vaṃ, Ghaṃ, Puṃ, Śaṃ, Caṃ, and Ḍaṃ:
Gaurī is in the east, Caurī in the south, Vetālī resides in the west,
Ghasmarī in the north, and likewise Pukkasī in the northeast.
Śavarī is in the southeast corner, Cāṇḍālī is situated in the southwest, and Ḍombinī is in the northwest;
thus the circle of goddesses is complete.
The syllable of body, speech, and mind situated between two *hoḥ* sounds.
One should meditate upon this, called the "being of the Gandharvas," within the lotus of the Goddess.
When the Gandharva has entered [the practitioner], he should recollect the swift attainment;
he is then impelled by the goddesses of the corners with songs of exhortation.
Arise, O Bharaṭṭaka! Piteously cry out to me, protect me!
Abandon desire for the union of great bliss; [behold] the nature of emptiness.
Even if you are struck down, I shall die; arise, O Hevajra!
Cast off this void-like bliss; let the task of the Śavarī be accomplished.
O Lord of the Gods, having invited me, why do you remain silent?
I am a Caṇḍālī; I entreat you, for without you, I cannot endure it.
"O Indīāhī, arise! I know your heart. We are *ḍombinīs* who cut the mind; do not cause a fracture in my compassion."
The Song of Exhortation: Awakened by the exhortation, one should recollect one's previous vow.
From the two *aṃhūṃ*s, the Great Vajrin arises in a fluid form.

Eight-faced, four-legged, and adorned with sixteen arms, he tramples upon the four Māras and performs the dance in the half-lotus posture (*ardhaparyaṅka*). He is decorated with a garland of severed heads and a necklace; his head bears a universal vajra (*viśvavajra*).
The central face is deep black, the right is like a kunda flower,
the left is red and most terrifying, and the remaining faces resemble bhr̥ṅga bees;
it is enriched with twenty-four eyes and bestows happiness upon Nairātmyā.
Likewise, elephants, horses, donkeys, cows, camels, humans, leopards,
and otters are to be known as being on the right-hand eight potsherds, in order, starting from the two-footed.
Earth, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Fire, the Moon, and the Sun,
as well as Antaka and Dhanada, [are located] in the skull-bowl on the left side of the eightfold [mandala].
Gaurī shall be black in color, Caurī resembles madder-red;
Vetālī has the luster of molten gold, and Ghasmarī is like the color of vermilion.
Pukkasī has the luster of sapphire; Śavarī has the radiance of a moonstone; Caṇḍālī is dark blue like the sky; and Ḍombinī is considered to be the color of a kunda flower.
In the right hand of Gaurī is a knife, and likewise a Rohitaka tree in her left;
in the right hand of Caurī is a fire-pan, and likewise a Sūkarakara tree in her left.
To the right of Vetālī is Kūrma; in her left hand she holds a skull-cup.
To the right of Ghasmarī is a serpent; from her left hand [also] issues a skull-cup.
The Pukkasi has a lion on her right [hand], and an axe is held in her left arm.
The mendicant bowl is prescribed on the right side of the Śavarī, and the water flask on the left.
The Cāṇḍālī has a wheel in her right hand and likewise a plow in her left;
the Ḍombinī has a vajra in her right hand and likewise a threatening gesture in her left.
Gaurī and the others are considered to have two arms, standing in the dance posture with one leg half-bent (ardhaparyaṅka).
They possess three eyes, their hair is upright, and they are adorned with the five mudrās.
[They trample upon] Brahmā, Indra, Upendra, Rudra, Vaivasvata, and the Lord of Wealth (Vittanāyaka).
Nairṛtī and Vemacitrī, as well as the detailed account of Gaurī and the others.
One should place the locus of gnosis (*jñānapada*) in the heart of all vajras;
the conceptualization of the seal-sign (*mudrācihna*) is accomplished from the syllables of one’s own mantra.
[This occurs] when [the practitioner] has reached the heart of the Gnosis-being (*jñānasattva*), which consists of the *hūṃ*-vajra upon the sun at the lotus of one’s own heart.
One should contemplate the *Hūṃ-jñānasattva* within a *Hūṃ-vajra* situated upon a lotus and sun;
having caused it to enter the *samaya-cakra*, the *sthāna-cakra* becomes intensely radiant.
Buddhahood and the state of a Bodhisattva are accomplished in this way, and not otherwise.
Commanded by *jaḥ*, *hūṃ*, *vaṃ*, and *hoḥ*, one should attract the four goddesses beginning with Gaurī,
cause them to enter, bind them, and satisfy them.
One should place the three Vajras—delusion and the others—within the three locations of the eyes and so forth:
Mohavajrī should be in the two eyes; Dveṣavajrikā in the two ears;
Mātsaryakī is said to be in the nose; and Rāgavajrikā in the mouth.
In the body there should be Īrṣyāvajrī, and in the mind Nairātmyayoginī;
born from the first syllable of their names, they are auspicious, with two arms and one face,
holding a curved knife and a skull-cup in their hands, possessing various colors, and seated upon corpses.
In body, speech, and likewise mind, by means of the mantra *oṃ āḥ hūṃ*,
one should meditate upon the sky-farer (*khecarī*), the earth-farer (*bhūcarī*), and the one dwelling in the underworld (*pātālavāsinī*).
These yoginīs, born from the three families, possess the radiance of the vajras of body, speech, and mind.
Having emanated from the seed-syllable in one’s own heart rays of light in the form of goads,
one should summon the Buddhas, worship them, and request consecration:
“May you all, O Protectors, Tathāgatas, consecrate me!”
Then, by these Tathāgatas who have assumed the form of Heruka, [the following was done].
He is sprinkled with jars filled with the liquid of the five nectars held in his own hands; from that sprinkling, there is the sealing of Akṣobhya upon his crown.
By this very [mantra], one should further seal Gaurī and Pukkasī.
But with the Buddhas Amitābha and the rest as the jewels, the remaining six are arranged in pairs.
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the empowerment of all Tathāgatas.
In the skull-cup blazing with one's own mind,
there arises from the five hooks and the five seed-syllables the vajra of the fruit of the *rasanā* [tongue].
Śrī Hevajra licks the nectar:
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra that tastes the nectar of all the Tathāgatas.
The holder of the wheel (cakrī) should worship the wheel, preceded by himself, with the eight goddesses emerging [from his body] through various offerings of knowledge and ignorance and so forth:
*Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the worship of all Tathāgatas.*
With this hymn, the Yoginīs praise the Lord of the Cakra.
Surrounded by a host of yoginīs,
you have attained excellence within your own mind; by you,
the entire world, including all that is moving and unmoving, has been purified.
Awakening the sentient beings with a heart of compassion,
you perform your work within the conceptual proliferation of Māyā;
O Maṇiśrī Saṃheruka Vajra, may you be victorious!
Praise.
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of praise to all Tathāgatas.
The activity of passion for the Vajra, the visualization of the abode of the Buddhas,
the tasting of the nectar of empowerment, worship, and praise— these constitute the six limbs.
By meditating upon these six limbs, the yogi swiftly attains accomplishment.
Vairocana is the Peak; Akṣobhya, the Tathāgata, is the Consecration; Amitābha is the Taste of Nectar; Śrī Ratnasambhava is the Praise;
Amoghasiddhi is declared to be the Worship; and Vajrasattva is the Enamouring.
Through its proximity, this six-limbed accomplishment arises:
in the first stage it appears like a cloud; in the second, like smoke;
in the third, with the form of a firefly; and in the fourth, a blazing lamp.
But by the fifth [stage], there is always a light, stainless and resembling the sky;
thereafter, it becomes in an instant like the form of an illusion and like the form of a dream.
The Caṇḍālī, ignited at the navel, burns the five Tathāgatas;
it also burns Locanā and the others, and once they are burnt, the moon [in the form of] Haṃ drips.
When the yogi becomes weary from meditation, he should then recollect purity.
The eyes are red due to compassion, and the body is black due to a mind of loving-kindness.
The four bases of sympathy are known as his four feet;
the eight liberations are his faces, and the sixteen emptinesses are his arms.
By means of the [five] mothers, there are five Buddhas; he is wrathful for the sake of subduing the wicked.
The three eyes are the triple body (trikāya), and the bones are the four truths.

The aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is Vajrī; feeling (vedanā) is Guptagaurī; the aggregate of perception (saṃjñāskandha) is likewise Vārī; and in the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra) is Vajraḍākinī.
His consciousness is the selflessness of the aggregates from the perspective of ultimate reality;
these very [aggregates] proceed toward the state of the six limbs for the purification of the six sense bases.
Dveṣavajrā would be the water [element], and Rasavajrikā [the taste element].
Īrṣyāvajrā as well as Mohavajrā shall be Vajraḍākinī;
Mātsaryā is Guptagaurī, while the mind is Nairātmyayoginī.
Pṛthivī is known as Pukkasī, and the water element is remembered as Śavarī.
Tejas is to be known as Caṇḍālinī, and Vāyu is proclaimed as Ḍombī;
Gaurī is always declared to be in form (rūpa), and Caurī is proclaimed to be in sound (śabda);
Vetālī is in the portion of smell (gandha), and Ghasmarī has the nature of taste (rasa).
Bhūcarī is renowned for touch, and Khecarī arises from the *dharmadhātu*. From earth up to wealth (the element of water), all are established for the sake of accomplishing all wonders.
Indeed, the elephant [form] was assumed for the pacification of the diseases of sentient beings.
Cough, asthma, insanity, consumption, leprosy, scabies, as well as elephantiasis, spleen disease, and similar ailments, are proclaimed [to afflict those who are not focused]; therefore,
the practitioner of meditation should recite the mantra while remaining clothed in a single garment.

Oṃ! To the eight-faced one, whose upward-straying hair is tawny, who possesses twenty-four eyes and sixteen arms, whose body is like a dark cloud, who wears many garlands of skulls, whose mind is puffed up with cruelty, and who has fangs like a half-moon: slay, slay! Cause [them] to be slain, cause [them] to be slain! Roar, roar! Threaten, threaten! Dry up, dry up the seven oceans! Bind, bind the eight Nāgas! Seize, seize the enemies! Ha hā hi hī hu hū he hai ho hau haṃ haḥ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!
And one should constantly offer the bali-oblation for the pacification of all obstacles.

Oṃ! Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, Yakṣa, Bhūta, Agni, Vāyu, Rakṣasa, Candra, Sūrya, Mahādeva, Brahmā, Pātāla, and the eight serpents: enjoy this bali; smell the flowers, the incense, and the meat; fulfill all our purposes; remove obstacles and diseases. Oṃ! The syllable *ā* is the mouth of all phenomena because they are unarisen from the beginning. Oṃ ĀḤ HŪṂ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ.
By Durjayacandra, a bee for the honey of the lotus-clusters of the Devītantras awakened by the sun of the True Guru.
Having drunk that which was vomited forth as honey by the one to be accomplished (the deity),
may whatever merit has been produced here from the exertion in composing this *Śrīkaruṇābalasādhana* [be for the benefit of all].
May that [teaching] become the sole boat for the worlds to cross over the ocean of existence.
Thus ends this *Ṣaḍaṅgasādhana* (The Six-Limbed Sadhana) extracted by the Vajrācārya Durjayacandra.
By whatever merit has been attained by us through extracting the non-cakra and the beautiful cakra of the Yoginīs, may that [merit] lead all beings to the state of the Moon-endowed Durjaya.
She promised to remain until she had attained enlightenment.
Emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; mindfulness of body, sensation, mind, and phenomena.
